tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Schematic for AKI/AKD Follow up According to Level of Health Facility
tables.caption: AKI/AKD follow-up by severity: who follows up and when, from short stage 1 AKI (non-nephrology care) to stage 3D or prior CKD 4 (nephrology within 1 week) (ADQI schematic)
tables.content:
Follow-up after AKI/AKD, from least to most severe (left to right in the schematic; non-nephrology care providers at the mild end, nephrology at the severe end):
1. Stage 1 AKI of short duration (1 day); SCr normal or returns to baseline; hospital-limited event in a healthy patient → consider KAMPS bundle within 1 year.
2. Stage 1 AKI lasting 1-2 days; limited comorbidities; no prior CKD; SCr not returning to baseline → consider KAMPS in 6 months.
3. Prolonged stage 1 AKI (3-6 days) or stage 2 AKI of shorter duration (1-3 days); increasing comorbidities (advancing age); SCr persistently elevated (<25% above pre-existing baseline) → labs in the next 3-6 weeks with long-term KAMPS/nephrology appointment (within the next several months).
4. Prolonged stage 2 AKI with urine analysis showing injury (duration >7 days); multiple comorbidities (cancer, prior AKIs, mild CKD at baseline); SCr persistently elevated >25% above prior baseline in some recovery → labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology; appointment/KAMPS within weeks.
5. Prolonged stage 3 AKI and persistent other forms of AKI or kidney disease; history of prior AKI, significant CV disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and advanced CKD → labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology.
6. AKI stage 3D (dialysis), recovered and non-recovered; prior CKD 4; recurrent AKI/AKD → KAMPS or WATCH-ME labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology within 1 week.

Example: a patient with CKD G4, regardless of AKI severity, should be followed by a nephrologist within 1 week. Abbreviations: 3D, dialysis; SCr, serum creatinine; UA, urine analysis; WATCH-ME, weight assessment, access, teaching, clearance, hypotension, medications; KAMPS (kidney function, awareness, medications, pressure, sick-day protocol). Reproduced from Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative (ADQI) XXII.
source_flags: '<2% 5 of pre-existing baseline' printed; read as <25%. 'KAPMS' and 'KAMPS' are both used; neither is defined in full (the legend gives 'pressure-sick day protocol').

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Requirements for AKI screening by level of health facility
tables.caption: AKI screening requirements by level of health facility: primary care clinic, health centre/regional hospital, tertiary care

body.t:
- Vital signs
- Weight (kg)
- Height (m or cm)
- Urine dipstick
- Good history & physical exam
- Medication & OTC review

- Includes all primary care assessments
- Urine analysis
- Urine microscopy, culture & sensitivity
- Blood tests: FBC, BUN, electrolytes, CO2/bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, glucose, LFTs, uric acid, HIV, hepatitis B & C, RPR
- Estimate GFR (Cockcroft-Gault if no lab eGFR)
- Blood cultures
- Abdominal ultrasound scan
- Cardiac monitoring

- Includes all health centre/regional hospital assessments
- Autoimmune serology (ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM)
- Myeloma screen (serum protein electrophoresis, urine Bence Jones proteins, serum free light chains)
- Urine stone analysis
- CT scan, intravenous pyelogram (IVP), urodynamic studies
- Urologist for de-obstruction
- Kidney biopsy (histopathology within 1 week)

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Patient Assessment
tables.caption: AKI patient assessment: vital signs targets, history, life-threatening effects, cardiac monitoring, ultrasound, urine analysis, chest X-ray

body.t:
- Pulse
- Blood pressure: aim MAP > 65 mmHg and < 110 mmHg (MAP = DBP + 1/3 PP; PP = SBP - DBP)
- Urine output: aim > 0.5 mL/kg/hour

- Presenting complaint
- Past medical, surgical, OBGYN, urology history
- Systems enquiry: nervous, musculoskeletal, endocrine, respiratory, cardiovascular, GI, ENT, dermatological
- Drug/toxin history (including OTC and herbal remedies)
- Urine output history
- Occupational history (e.g., laborer in hot weather)

- Pulmonary edema: SpO2, clinical signs, arterial blood gas (ABG)
- Hyperkalemia: ABG, electrolytes
- Metabolic acidosis: ABG
- ECG for hyperkalemia signs, LV hypertrophy, heart block, myocardial ischemia

- Exclude urinary tract obstruction (urgent de-obstruction needed)
- Assess kidney size (normal: 9–12 cm), appearance, and echogenicity

- Dipstick: specific gravity, protein, blood, leukocytes
- Microscopy: granular casts → ATN / GN; red cell casts / dysmorphic RBCs → RPGN; leukocytes → pyelonephritis / AIN

- Assess for fluid overload (pulmonary edema), cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion, or cardiomyopathy
- Exclude pulmonary-renal syndrome (look for infiltrates)

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Non-Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury
tables.caption: Non-pharmacological management of AKI by level of care: primary care clinic vs health centre and hospitals

header.t: Health Center, Regional Hospital, Referral Hospital

body.t:
- Stop intake of all salt and potassium containing foods and fluids
- For dehydration (watch out for tachycardia, hypotension, capillary refill > 2 seconds, low jugular venous pressure, dry armpits): encourage fluid intake, to 10 mL/kg/day plus visible fluid losses, to avoid fluid overload
- Remove nephrotoxic medications
- Avoid fluid overload in heart failure and advanced kidney failure
- Avoid nephrotoxins – avoid use of herbal remedy mixes

- As previous PLUS:
- Give oxygen, and nurse in semi-Fowler's position if patient has respiratory distress
- Adequate nutritional support: enough energy and adequate protein. Consider enteral/parenteral nutrition
- Monitor fluid input and output
- MDT client care depending on underlying cause of AKI

source_flags: 'Encourage fluid intake, to 10 mL/kg/day plus visible fluid losses' for dehydration is printed as is; the sentence mixes rehydration with fluid restriction. Clinician to confirm.
The health centre column text spans the health centre, regional and referral hospital columns in the PDF.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury > Fluid Challenge/Inotropes
tables.caption: AKI fluid challenge and inotropes: adults (500 ml boluses up to 2 L, adrenaline infusion) vs children (oral rehydration by dehydration severity, 20 ml/kg bolus)

body.t:
Fluid bolus of 500 ml isotonic fluid (preferably Ringer Lactate) over 15 minutes and reassess (BP, pulse, JVP, urine output), up to a total of 2 litres, to achieve mean arterial pressure >65 mmHg.
Start inotropes if adequate fluid challenge but still hypotensive, to avoid fluid overload and ensure tissue perfusion, e.g. adrenaline 4 mg (4 amps) in 200 ml of N/S IV at 10 ml/hr.
REMEMBER to look for hypoglycaemia/sepsis/other associated complications and start treatment as indicated. Request Intensive Care Unit review urgently.

Rehydrate per protocol for age and body weight.
Mild dehydration: oral rehydration solution 5 ml (1 teaspoon) every 5 minutes to replace losses, OR 10 ml/kg body weight for each loose stool.
Moderate dehydration: 5 ml oral rehydration solution every 5 minutes to a total of 50-100 ml/kg body weight over 2-4 hours.
Severe dehydration and failed oral rehydration: start cautious rehydration with a bolus of 20 ml/kg isotonic fluid such as Ringer Lactate IV, followed by maintenance IV fluids per paediatric protocols.
URGENT REFERRAL FOR ICU CARE. DO NOT OVERHYDRATE, AS IT IS LINKED TO INCREASED MORTALITY.

tables.context_before: Adjunct therapies are directed by the underlying cause: crystalloids for rehydration (preferably balanced solutions such as Ringer Lactate); relieve obstruction urgently; treat sepsis; immunosuppression as directed; treat electrolytes (hypercalcaemia); treat right heart failure (diuretics); relieve intra-abdominal pressure. Furosemide stress test: IV furosemide 1 mg/kg (furosemide-naïve) or 1.5 mg/kg (already on it); >200 ml urine over the next 2 hours suggests intact tubular function and likely recovery; <200 ml predicts ongoing dysfunction that may need dialysis.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury > Hyperkalaemia in AKI
tables.caption: Hyperkalaemia (K ≥6 mmol/l) in AKI: adults vs children: calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, bicarbonate, salbutamol, potassium binder, furosemide, dialysis

body.t:
- Stabilize myocardium with bolus IV calcium gluconate 10% at 10 ml over 2 minutes (maximum 20 ml). DO NOT GIVE AT THE SAME TIME/SAME DRIP AS SODIUM BICARBONATE.
- Shift potassium with ONLY 5 units (five units) short acting insulin (Actrapid) in 50 ml of dextrose 50% over 30 minutes (higher insulin amounts can accumulate in kidney failure and cause dangerous hypoglycaemia).
- Shift with salbutamol nebulizer at 10-20 mg every 1-2 hours (MONITOR FOR TACHYCARDIA AND ARRHYTHMIAS).
- Potassium binder such as sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) 15 g mixed in 100 ml water once daily (CAUTION – DO NOT GIVE IF BOWEL PATHOLOGY).
- If overloaded, give furosemide IV 40-80 mg to aid urinary potassium loss.
- Urgent referral for dialysis, or acute peritoneal dialysis locally per protocol.

- Stabilize myocardium with bolus IV calcium gluconate 0.5 ml/kg over 2-5 minutes.
- Shift potassium with dextrose 10% at 5 ml/kg IV bolus; if severe hyperkalemia, dextrose 10% 5 ml/kg IV bolus + Actrapid (short acting insulin) 0.1 units/kg (ESSENTIAL TO CHECK GLUCOSE EVERY 15-30 MINUTES AND CORRECT IF LOWER THAN 4 MMOL/L).
- Shift potassium with sodium bicarbonate (8.4%) 1-2 mmol/kg IV over 5 minutes.
- Shift potassium with salbutamol nebulizer – 2.5 mg if <25 kg and 5 mg if >25 kg, given 1-2 hourly (MONITOR FOR TACHYCARDIA AND ARRHYTHMIAS).
- DO NOT GIVE KAYEXALATE TO CHILDREN, AS IT CAN CAUSE NECROTISING ENTEROCOLITIS.
- If fluid overloaded, give furosemide IV 1-2 mg/kg; can repeat after 6 hours (individual dose not to exceed 6 mg/kg).
- Urgent referral for dialysis, or acute peritoneal dialysis locally per protocol while awaiting transfer or specialist review.

source_flags: Children: Kayexalate is contraindicated here ('DO NOT GIVE'), while the paediatric AKI chart on p.203 gives calcium resonium (kayexalate) 1 g/kg 4-hourly. Clinician to confirm.
tables.context_before: If hyperkalemia (≥6 mmol/l): cardiac monitor (risk of bradycardia, asystole, and ventricular arrhythmias). Fluid overload in kidney failure: IV furosemide at high doses (at least 120 mg, maximum 500 mg in 24 hours in adults); oxygen; isordil 5 mg sublingually; IV nitrate; morphine 2.5 mg IV titrated, maximum 10 mg, monitoring BP; urgent dialysis (referral to a centre with haemodialysis).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury > Clinical contexts for fluid administration in patients with or at risk of AKI
tables.caption: Clinical contexts for fluid administration in patients with or at risk of AKI: reasons, benefits, challenges and risks by age, setting, comorbidity and acute condition

header.t: Reasons for fluid administration and potential benefits
Challenges and risks of fluid administration

body.t:
- Diseases with volume losses
- Indications likely to be context-dependent

- Narrow window between hypovolemia and fluid overload
- Clear adverse effects of fluid overload
- Adverse effects of 'one size fits all' approach to fluid management
- Uncertain definition of clinically significant fluid overload
- In patients with heart disease, poor cardiac reserve to tolerate hypovolemia and hypervolemia
- In patients with diastolic dysfunction, risk of potentiating venous hypertension and renal congestion in fluid overload

- Specific conditions including diarrheal illness
- Impetus toward early resuscitation
- Dynamic phases of illness associated with hypovolemia

- Differing spectrum of disease
- Potentially delayed presentation to secondary care
- Limited range of therapeutic options
- Lack of advanced hemodynamic monitoring
- Inappropriate administration of maintenance fluid
- Risk of 'fluid-creep' leading to insidious fluid overload
Comorbid diseases: CKD; CHF or severe valvular disease

- Inability to conserve salt and water
- Poor cardiac reserve to tolerate hypovolemia

- Risk of hypovolemia
- Inability to handle fluid excess
- Predisposition to AKI
- Potentiation of adverse effects of fluid overload
- Potentially pre-existing interstitial edema
- Higher CVP associated with worsening kidney function
- Precipitation of fluid accumulation
Acute conditions: dehydration, hypovolemia, hemorrhage, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, major surgery, nephrotoxic exposure, abdominal compartment syndrome, ARDS, rhabdomyolysis/crush injury

- Acute free water deficit
- Salt and water deficit
- Acutely impaired oxygen delivery
- Intravascular hypovolemia
- Inability to tolerate hypovolemia
- Venodilation due to inotropic drugs
- Anesthesia-induced venodilation and vasodilation
- Perioperative fluid losses
- Dilution of filtered toxins
- Maintenance of visceral and renal perfusion
- Reduced cardiac preload due to high intrathoracic pressure
- Dilution of myoglobin
- Intravascular hypovolemia due to fluid losses to injured muscle

- Challenges of managing relative water and sodium deficits
- Need for consensus on optimal endpoints of resuscitation
- Dilution of hemoglobin may offset effects of fluid resuscitation on oxygen delivery
- Endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, fluid losses to interstitium and vasodilation
- Lack of evidence for goal-directed hemodynamic therapy
- Risk of pulmonary edema
- Association between high CVP and adverse kidney outcome
- Inappropriate administration of maintenance fluid and 'fluid creep' leading to insidious fluid overload
- Risk of fluid overload
- Risk of venous hypertension
- Risk of worsening alveolar edema
- Development/worsening of compartment syndrome

- Prevention of progression to overt AKI
- Reversal of early AKI

- Presence of early renal injury does not signify need for volume replacement
- Inappropriate attempts to 'reverse' established AKI resulting in fluid overload
- Oliguria as an indication of acute compensated hypovolemia

- Multiple etiologies of oliguria beyond hypovolemia
- Vicious cycle of fluid overload resulting in worsening kidney function

tables.caption: Complications of acute kidney injury: short term (fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemia, hypocalcaemia, drug toxicity) and long term (CKD, mortality, CV risk)

body.t:
1. Fluid overload related – pulmonary edema, hypertension
2. Electrolyte related – hyperkalemia with risks of bradycardia and asystole or ventricular fibrillation
3. Metabolic acidosis – Kussmaul respiration
4. Uraemic – uraemic pericarditis (risk of tamponade, especially following haemorrhagic conversion from heparin use during haemodialysis); uraemic encephalopathy (tremor, confusion, coma, seizures)
5. Electrolyte related – may have hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany – though commoner in CKD)
6. Systemic toxicity from accumulation of renally cleared pharmacologic agents – e.g. gadolinium, ethambutol

2. Worsening of underlying CKD

4. Cardiovascular risk

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pregnancy-Related AKI > Causes of PR-AKI
tables.caption: Causes of pregnancy-related acute kidney injury by trimester and postpartum (timeline), with disease-specific treatment and management of PR-AKI
tables.content:
Timeline of causes (bars across first, second, third trimester and postpartum):
- First trimester: hyperemesis gravidarum; septic abortion.
- Glomerulonephritis: from the first trimester through the third trimester.
- Urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis: late first trimester through the second and early third trimester.
- Preeclampsia/eclampsia/HELLP syndrome: from the second trimester into early postpartum.
- Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: second and third trimester.
- Placental abruption/haemorrhage: late second and third trimester.
- Obstruction: second and third trimester.
- Acute fatty liver: third trimester and postpartum.
- Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome: third trimester and postpartum.

Disease-specific treatment of AKI in pregnancy:
| Cause | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Hyperemesis gravidarum/prerenal causes | Hydration |
| Septic abortion/urinary tract infection | Antibiotics |
| Preeclampsia/HELLP/acute fatty liver of pregnancy | Delivery |
| Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura | Plasma exchange, rituximab |
| Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome | Eculizumab |
| Obstructive uropathy | Analgesics, stent, nephrostomy |
| Placental abruption and haemorrhage | Control bleeding, delivery |
| Glomerulonephritis | Steroids, immunosuppression |

HELLP: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets.
Management of PR-AKI: 1. risk reduction – close monitoring and hydration for hyperemesis gravidarum; 2. monitor for urosepsis and treat early; 3. reduce pre-eclampsia risk in patients with underlying CKD – aspirin, calcium, BP control.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Causes of CKD
tables.caption: Causes of chronic kidney disease by category: vascular, glomerular, tubulointerstitial, structural, others (CKDu, COVAN, chronic infections)

body.t: Hypertension, vasculitis etc. Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis, Takayasu's arteritis, fibromuscular dysplasia etc.
Diabetes, autoimmune diseases (e.g. lupus nephritis), chronic systemic infections (e.g. HIV, HBV, syphilis), drugs, neoplasia, glomerulonephritis, glomerulopathies

UTI, drug-induced interstitial nephritis (e.g. traditional herbs (timbita), rifampicin, allopurinol, fluoroquinolones, sulphonamides, beta-lactam antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, NSAIDs), infective, autoimmune, toxins, neoplasms e.g. myeloma
Hereditary - polycystic kidneys, renal masses, obstruction (stones, strictures), CAKUT in children (congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract)

Congenital - other congenital diseases (glomerular or tubular), e.g. Alport's syndrome. CKDu – CKD of unknown etiology amongst laborers in hot climates with no other traditional CKD risk factors (? due to heat and dehydration). COVAN – COVID-19 nephropathy with proteinuria. Chronic infections – HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, malaria etc. (can affect all areas of renal parenchyma). Chronic obstruction/posterior urethral valves (developmental)/vesicoureteric reflux (developmental), nephrolithiasis (kidney stones)

footnotes: A previous episode of acute kidney injury or acute kidney disease can lead to CKD; therefore all patients with a history of AKI require follow-up of renal function.
Many causes are potentially preventable or modifiable if detected early.
tables.context_before: Chronic kidney disease is structural or functional kidney damage present for >3 months, with or without a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Measuring kidney function
tables.caption: Measures of kidney function: direct measures (creatinine clearance, measured GFR), estimating equations for adults and children (Cockcroft-Gault, MDRD, CKD-EPI, FAS, Schwartz), and limitations

header.t: Indirect measures of kidney function: estimating equation

body.t:
- No estimate of kidney function has been specifically validated for glomerular disease and/or nephrotic syndrome
- Ethnicity is often a confounding influence
- In creatinine-based formulas, hypoalbuminemia may lead to overestimation of true GFR due to increased tubular creatinine secretion (8)
- Glucocorticoids may increase serum cystatin C, potentially underestimating eGFR (9)
- Low muscle mass overestimates eGFR using creatinine-based formulae (10)
- AKI confounds all estimates, which are valid only in steady state
- Measured GFR*: inulin clearance (gold standard); radioisotopic plasma clearance (1): 125I-iothalamate, 99mTc-DTPA, 51Cr-EDTA; non-radioisotopic plasma clearance: iohexol (2)

Adults:
- Cockcroft-Gault (3): (140 - age) x weight [kg] (x 0.85 if female) / (serum creatinine [mg/dl] x 72)
- Modification of diet in renal disease (MDRD) equations (4) (not valid for eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)
- CKD-EPI creatinine equation (preferred); valid with eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2
- CKD-EPI cystatin C equations (5) (valid for eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)
- Full Age Spectrum (FAS) equation (7); valid even in eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2
Children:
- Schwartz equation and its modifications (6)
- Full-age spectrum (FAS) formulae (7)

footnotes: Assessment of kidney function in glomerular disease. *In ml/min per 1.73 m2. The correct coefficient for race in GFR estimating equations is controversial (see the KDIGO CKD guideline). References: 1 Perrone et al.; 2 Gaspari et al.; 3 Cockcroft and Gault; 4 and 5 Stevens et al.; 6 Schwartz et al.; 7 Pottel et al.; 8 Branten et al.; 9 Zhai et al.; 10 Levey et al. CKD-EPI, Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration; 51Cr-EDTA, chromium-51 labelled ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid; 99mTc-DTPA, technetium-diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Screening and Diagnosis of Chronic Kidney Disease > Screening Algorithm for Kidney Disease
tables.caption: Screening algorithm for chronic kidney disease: who to screen, tests, CKD criteria, and lifestyle, medical treatment and other considerations
tables.content:
1. Area population:
   - No markers of risk: do not screen; rescreen based on future patient assessment.
   - Risk factors (high blood pressure; diabetes; cardiovascular disease; family history of CKD): screen.
2. Tests: blood glucose; spot urine; blood pressure; family history. Measure kidney function (serum creatinine or cystatin C; calculate eGFR) and kidney injury (albuminuria/proteinuria).
3. Do the results indicate CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 or albuminuria/proteinuria, ACR >30 mg/mmol as printed)?
   - No: rescreen based on future patient assessment.
   - Yes:
     - Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation; well-balanced diet; regular exercise; limit sodium intake to <2 g/day.
     - Medical treatment: blood pressure, diabetes and lipid control: ACEi/ARB therapy; SGLT2 inhibition; metformin; statins.
     - Considerations: drug dosing; contrast media use; hyperkalemia; CKD/CVD factors: anaemia, bone disease, heart failure, other (hepatitis C, metabolic acidosis, etc.).
     - Retesting; follow-up office visits; referral to a nephrologist when appropriate.
source_flags: The CKD threshold is printed 'ACR > 30mg/mmol'; elsewhere (pp.211, 215) albuminuria is ACR >30 mg/g or >3 mg/mmol. Clinician to confirm.
'Serum creatine', 'Albu,inuria' printed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Algorithm to screen, risk stratify and treat CKD
tables.caption: Algorithm to screen, risk-stratify and treat CKD (KDIGO-based): conditions of CKD risk, testing, classification, patient safety by eGFR, slowing progression and complications, CVD risk reduction, and when to refer to nephrology
tables.content:
1. Conditions of CKD risk: hypertension; diabetes; cardiovascular disease; AKI/hospitalisation history; family history of kidney disease; obesity; older age*; other high-risk comorbidities, environmental exposures, or genetic factors.
2. Consider screening for CKD: urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) to detect albuminuria; serum creatinine and cystatin C to estimate GFR.
3. Is any of the following present for 3 months or more: eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m²; ACR >30 mg/g (3 mg/mmol); markers of kidney disease?
   - No: periodically repeat evaluation.
   - Yes: classify/risk-stratify the CKD stage; identify and treat the specific cause of CKD.
     - eGFR category (ml/min/1.73 m²): G1 ≥90; G2 60-89; G3b 30-44; G4 15-29; G5 <15 (G3a is not listed).
     - Albuminuria category: A1 (normal or mild) <30 mg/g or <3 mg/mmol; A2 (moderate) 30-300 mg/g or 3-30 mg/mmol; A3 (severe) >300 mg/g or >30 mg/mmol.

Patient safety (all patients with eGFR <60): dose medications based on eGFR; reduce the risk of AKI from volume depletion; adopt 'sick day rules' as needed; avoid dual ACEi and ARB blockade; prevent contrast-associated AKI (lowest possible radiocontrast dose; adequate hydration before, during and after the procedure, consider isotonic saline; withhold ACEi or ARBs, diuretics and other nephrotoxic agents before and after the procedure).
- eGFR 45-59: avoid prolonged NSAIDs.
- eGFR 30-44: avoid prolonged NSAIDs; use metformin with close monitoring at 50% dose.
- eGFR <30: avoid any NSAIDs; avoid bisphosphonates; avoid metformin; avoid PICC lines (access preservation); if on warfarin, monitor PT-INR closely given increased risk of bleeding.

Slowing CKD progression and reducing complications:
- Treat high blood pressure: ACEi or ARB if ACR >30 mg/g or 3 mg/mmol; diuretic often required; dietary sodium <2000 mg/day.
- Type 2 diabetes: target HbA1c <6.5% to <8.0%; metformin for those with CKD and type 2 diabetes; if the glycaemic target is not achieved with metformin and SGLT2 inhibition, add a GLP1-RA.
- CKD complications testing: anaemia – evaluate if CKD G3-G5 and Hb <13 g/dl (men) or <12 g/dl (women); treat iron deficiency first; consider erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) if Hb 9-10 g/dl (avoid Hb >11.5 g/dl). Acidosis – correct to the normal range with bicarbonate supplementation if bicarbonate <22 mmol/l in CKD G3-G5. CKD-mineral bone disease – in CKD G3-G5 check calcium, phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D and intact PTH; supplement vitamin D deficiency.
- Influenza vaccination; pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccination in CKD G4-G5; screen for hepatitis C.

Reduction of CVD complications: CKD = CVD risk; systolic blood pressure target <120 mm Hg* (consider <130/80 mm Hg in kidney transplant recipients); start lipid-lowering therapy (CKD and age ≥50 years: statin recommended; CKD and age 18-49: statin if known CAD, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke, or high ASCVD risk); aspirin for secondary prevention unless bleeding risk outweighs benefits.

When to refer to nephrology: AKI or abrupt sustained fall in GFR; eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m²; consistent significant albuminuria (ACR >300 mg/g or 30 mg/mmol); progression of CKD; urinary red cell casts or RBC >20 per high-power field, sustained and not readily explained; CKD and hypertension refractory to 4 or more antihypertensive agents; persistent abnormalities of serum potassium; recurrent or extensive nephrolithiasis; hereditary kidney disease.

Notes (from the caption): based on KDIGO and adapted from Vassalotti et al. Care for older adults or those with limited life expectancy should be individualised. If eGFR (creatinine) is 45-59 ml/min per 1.73 m2, or in low muscle mass, chronic illness or malnutrition, order cystatin C to estimate GFR. There are no evidence-based recommendations on screening frequency; consider risk equations (e.g. CKD Prognosis Consortium). The systolic target <120 mm Hg is a level 2 recommendation; many patients may opt for a less intensive approach.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Pharmacological management of CKD to slow progression
tables.caption: Interventions to slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular risk by GFR and albuminuria stage (lifestyle, smoking, RAS inhibition, BP, statins, glycaemia, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 RA, metabolic acidosis)
tables.content:
Chart of interventions across CKD stages G1-G5 (each split A1-A3); bars show where each applies:
- Lifestyle modification: all stages.
- Smoking cessation: all stages.
- RAS inhibition (a): G1 to G4/G5 (shaded lighter in G5).
- Optimize blood pressure control: all stages.
- Statins (b): all stages (lighter in G5).
- Optimize glycemic control: all stages.
- SGLT2 inhibitors (c): G1 to G4, continued (dotted) into G5.
- GLP-1 receptor agonists (d): all stages.
- Treat metabolic acidosis: G3b to G5.
- Treat underlying cause, avoid nephrotoxins, and adjust medication dosages: all stages.

Notes: (a) Unclear if and when to discontinue renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition in advanced CKD. (b) Statins should be initiated for those beginning dialysis therapy (as printed); patients already receiving statins at dialysis initiation can continue them. (c) Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. An SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended as first-line treatment with metformin and may also benefit persons with CKD and no diabetes. SGLT2 inhibitors should be initiated if eGFR ≥30 ml/min and can be continued through G4-G5 until dialysis initiation, when they should be stopped; there is no evidence for starting SGLT2 inhibitors if eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2. (d) Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. A GLP-1 receptor agonist can be considered when an SGLT2 inhibitor and/or metformin is not tolerated or the glycaemic target is not reached. Dulaglutide can be used if eGFR >15 ml/min per 1.73 m2; exenatide if creatinine clearance >30 ml/min; there are limited data for liraglutide, lixisenatide or semaglutide in severe CKD. Consult dosing recommendations in CKD G4 and G5.

Also: treat anaemia (investigate the cause to exclude non-CKD causes), aiming for Hb 10-12 g/dl.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD and Diabetes > Glucose-lowering agents in CKD
tables.caption: Glucose-lowering agents in CKD and type 2 diabetes compared: effect on CKD progression, ASCVD, heart failure, glucose-lowering efficacy, hypoglycaemia risk, weight and cost
footnotes: Colour key in the PDF: neutral; potential benefit or intermediate glucose-lowering efficacy; benefits (organ protection, high efficacy, low hypoglycemia risk, weight loss, or low cost); potential risk or high cost to patient; increased risk of adverse effects.
(a) Benefit supported by primary and secondary outcome data. (b) Benefit supported by secondary outcome data. (c) Benefit or risk is agent specific.
ASCVD, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; CKD, chronic kidney disease; DPP-4, dipeptidyl peptidase 4; GLP-1, glucagon-like peptide 1; SGLT2, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2; T2D, type 2 diabetes.
source_flags: The footnote markers in the table are letters (a-c) but the footnotes are numbered 1-3; matched in order.
α-glucosidase inhibitors have no glucose-lowering efficacy printed.
tables.context_before: Glucose-lowering agents usable in CKD: metformin up to eGFR ≥30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (lactic acidosis reported with lower eGFR; reduces CV risk; check B12 after 4 years). SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) are recommended in diabetic and non-diabetic kidney disease to slow CKD progression; can be used in CKD4. GLP1-RAs are cardioprotective and reduce albuminuria and GFR decline in diabetic kidney disease; some can be used in CKD4. Non-renally cleared sulphonylureas such as gliclazide may be used cautiously (hypoglycaemia still possible). DPP4 inhibitors can be used in CKD1-5; thiazolidinediones (some agents) in CKD1-5; alpha glucosidase inhibitors up to CKD3b. Glucose may 'normalize' in advanced diabetic nephropathy.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Management in Special Populations > (h) CKD in pregnancy
tables.caption: CKD in pregnancy: maternal effects and effects on the foetus; pre-eclampsia risk reduction (aspirin, calcium)

body.t:
- Worsening of kidney function (higher risk if worse baseline kidney function, GFR <40 ml/min/1.73 m² and proteinuria >1 g/d; less if mild with little or no proteinuria and normal BP)
- Proteinuria (which can worsen kidney disease)
- Hypertension with risk of pre-eclampsia

- Intra-uterine growth retardation (IUGR) = low nephron mass = future risk of kidney disease & hypertension in baby
- Pre-term deliveries
- Teratogenicity (RAAS inhibitors)

tables.context_before: CKD in pregnancy requires co-management by an obstetrician and a nephrologist.
tables.table_note: Pre-eclampsia risk reduction in CKD: aspirin 81-150 mg OD (increases vascular relaxant prostacyclin and reduces thrombogenic/vasoconstrictive thromboxane A2; trials suggest some benefit); calcium 1.5-2 g daily may help those with low calcium levels.

tables.caption: CKD in children: definition, key points, and major causes under and over 5 years of age

body.t: Congenital malformations: hypoplastic/dysplastic kidneys; reflux nephropathy; obstructive uropathy; posterior urethral valves
Glomerular disease: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; hemolytic uremic syndrome; chronic glomerulonephritis; Alport's syndrome
Metabolic/genetic disorders: oxalosis; polycystic kidney disease; congenital nephrotic syndrome; Wilms' tumor
Tubulointerstitial disease: chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis; cystinosis; nephronophthisis; nephrotoxic drugs

tables.context_before: Definition of CKD in children: (1) kidney damage for ≥3 months, shown by structural or functional abnormalities of the kidney, with or without decreased GFR, with one or more of: abnormalities in the composition of the blood or urine; abnormalities in imaging tests; abnormalities on kidney biopsy; or (2) GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months, with or without other signs of kidney damage. Recognise children in the early stages of CKD; regular monitoring allows control of factors that aggravate progression. The main treatable causes of CKD in children in developing countries are urinary tract abnormalities, acute kidney injury and nephrotic syndrome. Identify the cause to plan management and prognosis. Major causes are congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract, reflux nephropathy, inherited disorders, glomerular diseases, renal stones, secondary to AKI, and haemolytic uraemic syndrome/thrombotic microangiopathy.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD and Contrast Media
tables.caption: CKD and contrast media: effect on the kidneys and management for gadolinium (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), iodinated contrast, and acute phosphate nephropathy

body.t: Exposure to high phosphorus levels in the presence of renal insufficiency. Usually reported following bowel preparation (e.g. for colonoscopy) with sodium phosphate containing solutions

Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis: a fibrosing disorder of the skin and viscera/systemic organs, secondary to gadolinium-based contrast agents in patients with acute and chronic renal insufficiency. First reported in patients with ESRD and AKI in 2006 (gadolinium is excreted unchanged by the kidneys)

Direct toxic effect on renal tubules, disrupting mitochondrial function, with generation of free radicals, causing apoptosis. Vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow through the medulla, with resultant ischaemia

Acute presentation with severely elevated serum phosphorus levels and AKI. Gradual worsening of renal function over weeks and months. Renal biopsy shows tubulointerstitial calcium and phosphorus deposition and damage

Avoid in CKD stage G5, but some risk in G4. If needed, counsel the patient and arrange dialysis immediately after the procedure and for up to 2 days after (based on gadolinium pharmacokinetics) to remove the gadolinium

Hold exacerbating drugs on the day of use, e.g. metformin, diuretics. Pre- and post-hydrate with normal saline 1 ml/kg/hour or 100 ml/hour for 3-12 hours before and after contrast (lower rates if risk of pulmonary oedema). Use low-volume contrast that is not hyper-osmolar

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Classification of Acute Glomerulonephritis
tables.caption: Classification of glomerulonephritis: non-proliferative (minimal change, membranous, FSGS) vs proliferative (IgA, membranoproliferative, RPGN, post-infectious, vasculitic, Goodpasture's), features and treatment
tables.content:
Glomerulonephritis is classified as non-proliferative (these tend to cause nephrotic syndrome) or proliferative.
A. Non-proliferative:
- Minimal change glomerulonephritis: abnormal podocytes seen on electron microscopy. Treat with supportive care + prednisolone; most respond well.
- Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN): thickened glomerular basement membrane; usually idiopathic. 1/3 have chronic MGN, 1/3 go into remission, 1/3 progress to renal failure.
- Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: segments of glomeruli develop sclerosis; presents with nephrotic syndrome; genetic causes identified; steroids often ineffective; 50% progress to renal failure.
B. Proliferative:
- IgA nephropathy: most common type of GN in adults; macroscopic haematuria appearing 24-48 hrs after URTI/GI infection; IgA deposits seen in the mesangial matrix.
- Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: primary (immune mediated) or secondary (SLE, hepatitis); usually progresses to end-stage renal failure.
- Post-infectious glomerulonephritis: occurs weeks after URTI, usually Strep pyogenes; supportive treatment; resolves over 2-4 weeks.
- Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis:
  - Vasculitic disorders: Wegener's granulomatosis (vasculitis of lungs, kidney and other organs; c-ANCA positive; treat with steroids + cyclophosphamide); microscopic polyangiitis (small vessel vasculitis; p-ANCA positive; treat with long-term steroids +/- cytotoxic agents).
  - Goodpasture's syndrome: autoimmune, anti-GBM antibody; glomerulus and lung affected; haematuria and haemoptysis; treat with steroids +/- steroid-sparing agents.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Screening and Diagnosis of Acute Glomerulonephritis
tables.caption: Acute glomerulonephritis / nephrotic syndrome: investigations and differential diagnosis (primary, secondary, genetic, systemic, inflammatory and other causes)

body.t:
- Urine dipsticks
- Urinalysis with microscopy
- 24-hour urine protein
- Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine
- Full blood count
- Complement studies (C3, C4)
- Serum lipids
- Serum electrolytes
- Confirm the presence of nephrotic syndrome (albumin, cholesterol, urine dipstick & spot urine protein/creatinine ratio)
- Exclude an underlying systemic or exogenous cause of nephrotic syndrome that may require treatment (diabetes, HIV, VDRL, hepatitis B, lupus serology, ANA and anti-ds DNA antibody etc., underlying malignancy e.g. myeloma causing amyloidosis)
- Determine renal function (creatinine, GFR – note may be falsely low because of low muscle mass)
- Exclude complications of nephrotic syndrome (sepsis from urinary losses of immunoglobulins – e.g. ascitic tap; Doppler studies to exclude venous thrombosis)
- Determine the need for a kidney biopsy (e.g. in children: deteriorating kidney function, refractory proteinuria)

1. Primary nephrotic syndromes: minimal change disease (MCD); focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS); membranous nephropathy; membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
2. Secondary causes: systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy); amyloidosis; infections such as HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis; drug-induced nephropathy
3. Genetic and congenital disorders: Alport syndrome; congenital nephrotic syndrome
4. Systemic diseases: multiple myeloma; systemic vasculitis; sarcoidosis
5. Inflammatory and infectious causes: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease); post-infectious glomerulonephritis
6. Others: haematologic disorders – thrombotic microangiopathies like haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP); malignancies – some cancers cause paraneoplastic glomerulopathies

body.t: Urine albumin nil or trace (or proteinuria <4 mg/m2/h) for three consecutive days
Urine albumin 3+ or 4+ (or proteinuria >40 mg/m2/h) for three consecutive days, having been in remission previously

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Pharmacological Management of Glomerulonephritis > Nephrotic syndrome treatment
tables.caption: Nephrotic syndrome (children) treatment flowchart: initial prednisone, consolidation, and relapsing nephrotic syndrome (infrequent, frequent/steroid-dependent, steroid-resistant)
tables.content:
Initial episode:
1. Age 3-12 months or >12 years, gross haematuria, or low complement?
   - Yes: consider kidney biopsy.
   - No: intensive daily prednisone therapy 60 mg/m² (2 mg/kg).
2. Remission within 4 [weeks]?
   - No: consider kidney biopsy.
   - Yes: consolidation therapy (alternate-day prednisone) for 8 weeks: 40 mg/m² (~1.5 mg/kg) every 48 h for 4 weeks, then 20 mg/m² (~0.75 mg/kg) every 48 h for 4 weeks, then stop.

Relapsing idiopathic nephrotic syndrome:
- Infrequent relapses: prednisone 60 mg/m² daily until remission, then 40 mg/m² on alternate days for 4 weeks.
- Frequent relapses or glucocorticoid dependence:
  - Option 1: assess the alternate-day prednisone threshold. Threshold <15 mg/m² (<0.5 mg/kg) → remission → alternate-day prednisone (0.1 to <0.5 mg/kg/dose). If glucocorticoid toxicity or no remission → option 2.
  - Option 2: start a second-line agent if previous long-term glucocorticoid use with signs of toxicity.
- Glucocorticoid resistance: kidney biopsy; therapy based on histological diagnosis.
source_flags: 'Remission within 4' has no unit (weeks). 'Gross hematuria, complement' presumably means low complement. '(-1.5mg/kg)' printed for ~1.5 mg/kg.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Kidney Biopsy
tables.caption: When to do a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria (decision tree)
tables.content:
Decision tree for considering a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria:
- The kidney biopsy is the gold standard for diagnostic evaluation of glomerular diseases. Biopsy should be performed if the result is expected to modify treatment and/or if additional prognostic information is needed.
- Patients classically treated without a kidney biopsy diagnosis (children): steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome ≤12 years old; post-streptococcal GN.
- Examples of conditions for which treatment may be considered without diagnostic confirmation by kidney biopsy: PLA2Rab+ (membranous nephropathy); PR3+ ANCA vasculitis; anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; Alport disease; Fabry disease; familial focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis in families with well-characterised mutations; biopsy contraindicated as judged by history, physical exam and laboratory testing; systemic lupus erythematosus.

ANCA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; MPO, myeloperoxidase; PLA2Rab+, M-type phospholipase A2 receptor antibody positive; PR3, proteinase 3. Referral to a nephrologist may include immunosuppressive treatment such as prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, angiotensin blockade.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Pharmacological Management of Glomerulonephritis > Treatment algorithm for NS in a newly nephrotic child
tables.caption: Treatment algorithm for nephrotic syndrome in a newly nephrotic child: by age and syndromic features; steroid response; frequent relapser, infrequent relapser, steroid-dependent, non-responder
tables.content:
New nephrotic syndrome in a child:
- ≥12 years of age, syndromic features or family history (as printed; see flag): biopsy and/or genetic testing + referral to a specialty centre.
- ≤12 years of age, no syndromic features or family history: glucocorticoids* (oral prednisone or prednisolone).
  - No response after 4 or 6 weeks: genetic testing; kidney biopsy; calcineurin inhibitor; renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade.
  - Complete responder: glucocorticoids* for 8 or 12 weeks, then by course:
    - Frequent relapser: cyclophosphamide; levamisole; mycophenolate mofetil; rituximab; calcineurin inhibitor.
    - Infrequent relapser: glucocorticoids*.
    - Steroid-dependent: mycophenolate mofetil; rituximab; calcineurin inhibitor; cyclophosphamide.

Refer to a clinical trial where appropriate. NS, nephrotic syndrome. The management of glomerular disease depends on the type/cause and is individualised by a specialist according to the kidney biopsy histology.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Management in Special Populations > Glomerular disease in pregnancy
tables.caption: Coordinated care of pregnant patients with glomerular disease: prepregnancy, antenatal, delivery and postnatal actions

body.t:
- Discuss timing of contraception; contraception advice if needed; fertility assessment if needed
- Assess disease activity, with repeat biopsy confirmation if necessary; optimize blood pressure control
- Change to non-teratogenic medications and provide reassurance about continuation of safe medications
- Explain the risk of pregnancy complications and the need for heightened surveillance

- Target BP <140/90 mmHg
- Oral glucose tolerance test (especially important in women taking glucocorticoids or calcineurin inhibitors)
- Start low dose aspirin; consider vitamin D and calcium supplements
- Frequent fetal monitoring if concerns about fetal well-being: up to twice weekly BPPs, up to placental Dopplers, 2-weekly growth scans
- Baseline and serial kidney function, proteinuria (albumin-creatinine or protein-creatinine ratios or 24h collections) and markers of disease activity
- Monitoring of calcineurin inhibitor levels if required
- Consider venous thromboembolism prophylaxis if risk factors, e.g. nephrotic syndrome, previous venous thromboembolic events, high body mass index

- Delivery if fetal or maternal decompensation
- NOT at a pre-specified gestation
- Glucocorticoids for fetal lung maturation at least 24 h and up to 7 d before anticipated delivery if <34 weeks gestation

- Encourage breastfeeding
- Careful surveillance for active glomerulonephritis
- Calcineurin inhibitor level if dose changed in pregnancy
- Continue venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for at least 6 weeks if necessary
- Emotional support

footnotes: Adapted from Blom K, Odutayo A, Bramham K, et al. Pregnancy and glomerular disease: a systematic review of the literature with management guidelines. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2017;12:1862-1872. BP, blood pressure; BPP, biophysical profile; q2, every 2.

tables.context_before: Epilepsy is a chronic noncommunicable brain disorder characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures (two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart). This module covers convulsive epilepsy. With proper treatment, most people can be seizure-free.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Epilepsy Algorithm of Assessment and Management
tables.caption: Epilepsy assessment and management algorithm: 8 assessment steps, emergency management of seizures >5 min, when to refer, first aid at home
tables.content:
Assessment:
1. Person presents with episodes of convulsions (fits, shaking, stiffening), witnessed or reported.
2. Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency?
3. Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal.
4. Assess: postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history?
5. Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age.
6. Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life.
7. Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety).
8. Diagnosis: epilepsy confirmed → proceed to management.

EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT (seizure > 5 min): call for emergency help immediately; diazepam 10-20 mg IV/PR or lorazepam 4 mg IV for status epilepticus; airway – place in recovery position, ensure breathing; DO NOT restrain; DO NOT put anything in the mouth; monitor blood glucose; give thiamine if alcohol-related.

When to refer: first seizure (confirm diagnosis); seizures not controlled after 2 drug trials; pregnancy + epilepsy (specialist input needed); status epilepticus; suspected structural cause (tumour, stroke).

First aid at home (advise carers): lay the person on their side, head turned to the side; ensure the airway is clear, loosen tight clothing; time the seizure and stay until fully conscious; no food/water until fully alert; seek help if the seizure lasts >5 min, there is no recovery, or injury; epilepsy is NOT contagious.
source_flags: 'First seizure' is a referral reason, while step 2 requires 2+ unprovoked seizures for diagnosis; both are printed.

tables.context_before: Antiepileptic medications: start one medication at the lowest dose and increase slowly until seizures are controlled. 1. Start low and go slow with a single AED as monotherapy, chosen by seizure type and epilepsy syndrome; titrate to the maximal dose. 2. If the first AED is ineffective at the maximum tolerated dose, introduce an alternative AED slowly without tapering the first. 3. If there is a good response to the second AED, consider withdrawing the original gradually. 4. If the first add-on AED is ineffective or has undesirable side effects, withdraw it slowly and replace it with another add-on AED. 5. If seizures are not controlled on two AEDs, some patients may benefit from a third. 6. Prefer an add-on AED with a different mode of action. 7. Review the diagnosis if seizures continue despite this approach and 2-3 years have elapsed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Psychoeducation, cautions and follow-up
tables.caption: Epilepsy psychoeducation and psychosocial interventions, cautions and special populations (drug interactions, pregnancy, children, PLHIV), and follow-up
tables.content:
Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions:
- Epilepsy is caused by abnormal electrical brain activity, NOT spirits or witchcraft.
- Chronic condition: medication controls seizures in most if taken daily.
- People with epilepsy can marry, work, have children and lead normal lives.
- Avoid open fires, swimming alone, heights, heavy machinery, alcohol excess.
- Observe local driving laws; may qualify for disability benefits.
- All AEMs: taper slowly; an abrupt stop causes breakthrough seizures.
- Review every 3-6 months; check adherence and side effects.

Cautions & special populations:
- Check drug-drug interactions: AEMs reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives and antiretrovirals.
- Rare: severe bone marrow depression, Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
- Pregnancy: consult a specialist; supplement folate; valproate contraindicated.
- Children: weight-based dosing; monitor growth and development.
- PLHIV: check interactions with antiretrovirals before prescribing.
- (Printed in the same cell:) minimum 2 years seizure-free before [stopping AEMs].

Follow-up (every 1-3 months initially, then 3-6 monthly): review seizure frequency (decreased or stopped?); check medication adherence and side effects; assess functional status (school, work, daily activities); screen for depression/anxiety comorbidity; if no seizures for 2+ years, discuss gradual tapering with a specialist; if seizures continue despite an adequate dose, increase the dose, check adherence, or refer to a specialist.
source_flags: 'minimum 2 years seizure-free before' is printed at the end of the PLHIV bullet; it presumably refers to stopping AEMs.
Valproate is 'contraindicated' in pregnancy here, while it is listed without a pregnancy warning in the drug table. The follow-up box continues on p.249.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Systematic approach to long-term pharmacological treatment
tables.caption: Systematic approach to long-term pharmacological treatment of epilepsy: when to start AEDs, monotherapy, second AED, referral, re-evaluation, surgery and other options
tables.content:
When to start AEDs: immediate AED therapy is usually not necessary after a single seizure; it is generally started after two or more unprovoked seizures.

1. Initial AED monotherapy. Select the AED based on seizure type/syndrome, age, sex, childbearing potential, comorbidities, concomitant medications, adverse effects, interaction profile.
2. If failure: second AED, as monotherapy or add-on.
3. If failure: referral to a tertiary care centre (a).
4. Diagnostic re-evaluation (epilepsy yes/no, seizure types, syndrome, adherence, dosing), then: resective surgery; additional drug trials; neurostimulatory and dietary approaches (b).
Options at tertiary level: epilepsy surgery; ketogenic diet; vagus nerve stimulation; deep brain stimulation.
source_flags: The footnotes (a) and (b) are not printed. 'sydrome' printed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Status Epilepticus > Treatment Algorithm for Status Epilepticus
tables.caption: Management algorithm for status epilepticus in adults (ICU): stabilisation 0-5 min, first-line benzodiazepines 5-15 min, second-line valproate or phenytoin 15-30 min, third-line anaesthetic infusions after 30 min
tables.content:
Epilepsy emergencies: (i) acute repetitive seizures; (ii) status epilepticus.

0-5 minutes (stabilisation):
1. Stabilise the patient: assess airway, breathing, circulation.
2. Time the seizure onset; monitor vital signs (ECG, BP, HR, temperature).
3. Finger-stick blood glucose. If glucose <60 mg/dl, give 50 ml of 50% dextrose IV.
4. Laboratory investigations: electrolytes, CBC, liver and renal function tests.
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

5-15 minutes (first-line therapy): IV diazepam ('0.5 - 0.2 mg/kg/dose' as printed), max 10 mg, OR IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max not printed).
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

15-30 minutes, on ward (second-line therapy): valproate (VPA) 30 mg/kg loading dose and 4-8 mg/kg every 8 hr maintenance, OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading dose and '1.5 mg' every 8 hr maintenance (as printed).
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

After 30 minutes, on ward (third-line therapy):
1. Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg bolus and 1-2 mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for a minimum of 24 hr.
2. Propofol 1-3 mg/kg bolus and 5-10 mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for 24 hr.
3. Thiopental 3-5 mg/kg bolus and '3-3 mg/kg/hr' continuous infusion for 24 hr (as printed).
source_flags: Several doses are misprinted: diazepam '0.5 - 0.2 mg/kg/dose' (usually 0.15-0.2 mg/kg); phenytoin maintenance '1.5 mg every 8hr' (no per-kg unit); thiopental infusion '3-3 mg/kg/hr'; lorazepam has no maximum. Propofol 5-10 mg/kg/hr is high for a 24 h infusion. Clinician to confirm.
Glucose threshold is in mg/dl (60 mg/dl ≈ 3.3 mmol/L) while the rest of the guideline uses mmol/L. 'Diazepan', 'bogus' (bolus), 'stablization' printed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Cervical Cancer > Cervical Cancer Screening & Treatment Algorithm
tables.caption: Cervical cancer screening and treatment algorithm: HIV-negative women vs women living with HIV (HPV DNA testing, VIA/VILI triage, screen-and-treat, stop age)
tables.content:
A. General population (HIV-negative women):
1. Age 25-50 years: HPV DNA testing; screen every 5 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 5 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every 2 years (rescreen in 2 years):
   - Negative: rescreen in 2 years.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/colposcopy.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

B. Women living with HIV:
1. HIV positive, age 25+ OR at diagnosis: HPV DNA testing; screen every 3 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 3 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every year or VILI every year (return in 1 year):
   - Negative: return in 1 year.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/oncology.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

Single-visit screen-and-treat: SCREEN → TRIAGE → TREAT (same day) → FOLLOW-UP; same-day care when feasible.
VIA: visual inspection with acetic acid. VILI: visual inspection with Lugol's iodine.
source_flags: In both panels the chart draws VIA as a routine screen after a negative HPV test (as well as a triage test after a positive one), and the HIV panel has a second 'Negative' box reading 'Refer for LEEP / Year'. The intended pathway is unclear; summarised here. Clinician to confirm.
Stopping screening at 50 in women living with HIV differs from usual WHO advice (continue screening); the age range for the general population is printed '25-50'.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Risk Stratification for Breast Cancer
tables.caption: Breast cancer risk stratification by family history and genetics: above average, moderately increased, high risk

body.t:
- No family history
- One first-degree relative or 1–2 second-degree relatives diagnosed at age 50 or older

- A first-degree relative diagnosed before age 50
- Two or more first-degree relatives on the same side of the family diagnosed at any age

- Known to carry a breast cancer susceptibility gene mutation (e.g. BRCA1 or BRCA2)

tables.table_note: General population screening should begin at age 35 with clinical and self-exam. High-risk clients start 8-10 years earlier than the index case (e.g. those with BRCA mutations may start at age 25). tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Recommended diagnostics for breast cancer
tables.caption: Breast cancer diagnostics: biopsy techniques, pathology, laboratory tests and radiology for staging

body.t:
- Biopsy techniques: excision; lumpectomy; tru-cut biopsy
- Ultrasound guided biopsies are preferred
- A full pathology report including immunohistochemistry (IHC)

- A full biochemistry report, including KFT and LFT
- FBC and differential count

- Echocardiogram report
- Contrasted CT scan to include chest, abdomen and pelvis to rule out metastasis
- Chest X-ray prior to surgery to rule out effusions
- Bone scan in locally advanced breast cancers on the radiologist's recommendation if CT does not show metastasis; diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with MRI to image the spine. Note: DWI is recommended in place of a bone scan if a bone scan is not available
- Bilateral mammogram required for every patient for staging: the mammogram should include bilateral and axillary ultrasound; lymph nodes: routine supraclavicular ultrasound

tables.context_before: Screening modalities: breast self-examination (breast awareness); clinical breast examination by a trained health worker; breast ultrasound; mammography; FNA; tissue biopsy (incision, excision or tru-cut); MRI in selected cases.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > How to Advise Client on Breast Self-Examination
tables.caption: Breast self-examination: how to advise clients (looking, touching, lying down, lymph nodes)
tables.content:
1. By looking: stand before a mirror and look at both breasts and nipples – once with both arms beside your body; once with both hands on your hips; once with both arms raised and arms behind your head.
2. By touching: raise your left arm. Use the pads of 3 or 4 fingers of the right hand to examine your left breast; repeat on the right side. Examine once in lines up and down the breast from outside and inside; once in circles around the breast, making smaller circles towards the nipple; once in wedges starting from outside towards the nipple and back again.
3. While lying down: lie on your back, left arm over your head and a pillow under your left shoulder. Examine your left breast with your right hand as described before; repeat for the right side. This position flattens the breast and makes it easier to examine.
4. Lymph nodes: place your left hand on your waist. With your right hand try to find enlarged lymph nodes in the left underarm area and around your collar bone; repeat on your right side. An enlarged lymph node feels like a corn kernel or a bean.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Clinical Breast Examination > What to look out for and palpation sequence
tables.caption: Clinical breast examination: what to look out for (lump, pulled-in nipple, dimpling, skin changes, redness/rash, discharge) and the palpation sequence
tables.content:
What to look out for during CBE (illustration): lump; pulled-in nipple; dimpling; skin changes; redness/rash; dripping (nipple discharge).

Sequence to follow when performing breast palpation: 1. upper outer quadrant; 2. upper inner quadrant; 3. lower inner quadrant; 4. lower outer quadrant; 5. nipple-areola area; 6. axillary (underarm) quadrant.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Early Referral Flow Chart for Suspected Breast Cancer
tables.caption: Early referral flowchart for suspected breast cancer: urgent referral to the specialised breast unit, booking, or surgical clinic, by likelihood of malignancy
tables.content:
Suspected lump → provider-initiated clinical breast exam (PI-CBE) and direct referral to the specialised breast unit (SBU):
- High likelihood of malignancy → URGENT REFERRAL TO SBU (call and inform the SBU): suspicious lump (fixed, hard, irregular); palpable axillary lymph node; ulceration; nodules on the skin; skin tethering; nipple retraction; nipple discharge (e.g. bloody).
- Unsure → book SBU: palpable lump in women >25 years; non-lactational breast infection/abscess.
- Unlikely to be malignant → book for surgical clinic: palpable lump in women <25 years; breast pain with normal PI-CBE; family history with normal PI-CBE; lactation-associated infection with non-resolution/recurrence.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Warning Signs of Childhood Cancers (St. Siluan's signs)
tables.caption: Warning signs of childhood cancers (St. Siluan's signs): seek help, eye, lump, unexplained symptoms, aches, neurological signs, with likely cancers and actions

body.t: Seek medical help early for ongoing symptoms: prolonged symptoms; symptoms persist after treatment; symptoms return after initially disappearing
Seek medical help; return to the same clinic/doctor for follow-up

White spot in the eye (leukocoria) → possible retinoblastoma; loss of red eye reflex; new squint or sudden blindness → possible brain tumour; bulging eyeball → possible eye cancer or retro-orbital tumour
Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist or paediatrician
Lump in the abdomen, pelvis, head, arms, legs, testicle or glands; Wilms' tumour (age 3–4 years); consider neuroblastoma, lymphoma
Refer every lump to a doctor. If treated for TB without confirmation and not improving after 2 weeks → re-evaluate, consider biopsy
Unexplained fever for over two weeks; weight or appetite loss; fatigue; pallor; easy bruising and bleeding
Possible leukaemia or solid tumours; requires thorough clinical assessment
Aching bones, joints, back and easy fractures. Aches and pains in bones and back are not common in children and should raise suspicion
Possible leukaemia or sarcoma; needs critical evaluation

Change in walk, balance or speech; regression of milestones; slurred speech; continuous headaches (>1 week) with or without vomiting; early morning vomiting; cranial nerve palsy; enlarged head (hydrocephalus)
Possible brain tumour; prompt referral and neuroimaging as needed

tables.context_before: Childhood cancers arise between birth and 19 years. A high index of suspicion and early detection are critical.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Childhood Cancer Referral Pathway
tables.caption: Childhood cancer referral pathway: primary clinic identification, urgent referral, workup, MDT, confirmation, paediatric oncology
tables.content:
1. Primary clinic (e.g. GP, school nurse): identify suspected cancer using the SILUAN signs (significant, unexplained, rapid onset, ongoing symptoms, night sweats).
2. Urgent referral to a health centre/regional hospital.
3. Initial workup and assessment: physical exam, blood tests, imaging as needed.
4. Multidisciplinary team (MDT): paediatric oncologist, radiology, radiotherapy (as printed 'ratiology'), pathology, surgery.
5. Confirmation of diagnosis.
6. Referral to paediatric oncology for management (treatment planning, supportive care).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Oral & Maxillofacial Cancers > Diagnostic Algorithm
tables.caption: Oral lesion diagnostic algorithm: clinical diagnosis, follow-up vs biopsy, adjuvant diagnostic techniques and urgent referral
tables.content:
Photographs show the steps of the oral examination.

1. Oral lesion → previous clinical diagnosis based on clinical data.
2. Lesion resolves with or without therapy → follow-up.
3. Lesion changes, persists or progresses → perform a biopsy → identification of the histological entity, with or without malignancy → follow-up (or repeat biopsy).

Adjuvant diagnostic techniques: 1. oral cytology; 2. salivary biomarkers; 3. light-based techniques (auto-fluorescence, spectroscopy, chemiluminescence); 4. tissue staining.

Diagnostic workup: if there is any suspicion that a lesion may be oral cavity cancer, document the lesion site and size, take a clinical photograph if possible, and make an urgent referral to an oral & maxillofacial surgeon who is part of a head and neck oncology MDT. Any oral lesion (including a patch or ulcer) that fails to resolve in 2-3 weeks should raise suspicion.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Prostate Cancer > Summary Guideline for Management by Risk Category
tables.caption: Prostate cancer management by risk category (very low, low, high risk): observation, active surveillance, radiotherapy, radical prostatectomy, hormone therapy

body.t: Life expectancy <10 yrs: observation. Life expectancy 10-20 yrs: active surveillance. Life expectancy >20 yrs: active surveillance, radiotherapy (EBRT or brachytherapy), or radical prostatectomy (RP) +/- pelvic lymph node dissection (LND) if >2% risk of LN involvement (Roach or Partin tables)
Life expectancy <10 yrs: observation. Life expectancy >10 yrs: RT alone, RP +/- pelvic LND, or active surveillance. If RP with positive margins → adjuvant RT (preferred) or expectant management

Radiotherapy (3DCRT/IMRT with IGRT +/- brachytherapy boost) + long-term hormone therapy (2-3 yrs; neoadjuvant, concurrent and adjuvant). 4-6 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) considered for select patients with a single adverse feature with Gleason score 6-7. Consider whole pelvis radiotherapy. Consider RP with pelvic LND only for selected patients with low-volume disease and no fixation. Adjuvant RT +/- short-term ADT for positive margins or pT3 disease

footnotes: ADT: androgen deprivation therapy; CAB: combined androgen blockade; EBRT: external beam radiation therapy; IGRT: image-guided radiation therapy; IMRT: intensity-modulated radiation therapy; LN: lymph node; LND: lymph node dissection; RP: radical prostatectomy; RT: radiotherapy; 3DCRT: three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy.
source_flags: The table has no intermediate-risk row (very low, low and high risk only). The first column is headed 'Stage' but lists risk categories.
tables.context_before: Management depends on stage, risk category, age, comorbidities and life expectancy, performance status, resources, hormone sensitivity in metastatic disease, and the patient's wishes. Options: watchful waiting; active surveillance; surgery (radical prostatectomy, TURP etc.); radiotherapy (external beam, brachytherapy); hormonal therapy (medical or surgical castration, bilateral orchiectomy); chemotherapy; supportive care (pain management, bisphosphonates such as zoledronate). Localised disease: radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy with or without hormones. Metastatic hormone-sensitive: bilateral orchiectomy (cheaper than medical therapy) or hormonal therapy as ADT or combined androgen blockade (CAB). Castration-resistant: second-line hormonal agents (enzalutamide, abiraterone) and/or chemotherapy (docetaxel).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Cataract > Screening and Diagnosis of Cataract
tables.caption: Cataract screening, diagnosis and management workflow: assessment, ruling out other causes, impact on daily life, referral, early vs significant cataract, surgery; referral rules
tables.content:
1. Patient presents with visual complaints: gradual, painless vision loss; glare, haloes, blurred vision.
2. Clinical assessment: visual acuity; lens exam (cloudiness); red reflex.
3. Rule out other causes of vision loss: retinal disease; glaucoma; refractive errors.
4. Confirm the cataract diagnosis.
5. Assess the impact on daily life: daily activities; bilateral/unilateral; uncorrectable with glasses.
6. Refer to an ophthalmologist: full evaluation; biometry.
   - Mild/early cataract: monitor; improve lighting; adjust glasses.
   - Affects daily life (significant cataract): surgery (phacoemulsification + IOL); post-operative care: eye drops, follow-up, patient education.

REFER ALL SEVERE/SIGNIFICANT CATARACT CASES TO AN EYE SURGEON FOR CATARACT SURGERY. Refer clients with comorbidities such as HTN/DM, and pregnant women with cataract, to an ophthalmologist once a year from diagnosis for routine screening. Refer children immediately: a white pupil in a child may be an eye tumour, and late referral may lead to permanent loss of vision, squint, loss of the eye or loss of life.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Management of Pain > WHO Analgesic Ladder
tables.caption: WHO analgesic ladder for adult pain: step 1 non-opioid (mild), step 2 weak opioid (moderate), step 3 strong opioid (severe), with drug categories
tables.content:
Pain scores on the numerical rating scale: none 0; mild 1-3; moderate 4-6; severe 7-10.
- Step 1, mild pain (0-3): non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
- Step 2, moderate pain (4-6): weak opioid +/- non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
- Step 3, severe pain: strong opioid +/- non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
Step up if pain persists or increases; step down if pain decreases.

Categories of drugs:
- Non-opioids: ibuprofen or other NSAID, paracetamol (acetaminophen), or aspirin.
- Weak opioids: codeine, tramadol, or low-dose morphine.
- Strong opioids: morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, buprenorphine.
- Adjuvants: antidepressant, anticonvulsant, antispasmodic, muscle relaxant, bisphosphonate, or corticosteroid.
Combining an opioid and a non-opioid is effective, but do not combine drugs of the same class. Time doses by drug half-life ('dose by the clock'); do not wait for pain to recur.

Low-dose morphine is given if the maximum weak-opioid dose does not work. No ceiling dose for morphine (increase gradually until pain is controlled). Pethidine can be used for acute pain (NOT for chronic pain)

tables.heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Palliative Care in the Trajectory of the Patient's Illness
tables.caption: Palliative care across the illness trajectory, and palliative care tasks by level (referral hospital, regional hospital, health centre/primary clinic, home)
tables.content:
Trajectory (diagram): from presentation/diagnosis, therapies to modify disease (curative, restorative intent) decrease over time while therapies to relieve suffering and/or improve quality of life (palliative care) increase; palliative care continues through life closure and active dying to death, followed by bereavement care.

Palliative care by level:
- Referral hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; holistic care with specialised management (radiotherapy, chemotherapy, surgery).
- Regional hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; initiate or adjust the PC regimen for mild, moderate or severe symptoms; plan continued PC after discharge to a lower level or home; refer to referral hospitals for specialised management.
- Health centre/primary care clinic: visit the patient at home in the first week after discharge if possible; holistic pain assessment; pain and symptom management using the WHO ladder; emotional support; liaise with CHWs who visit patients at home; request oral morphine solution for PC patients in the HC catchment area; request advice from the regional hospital if needed; refer complicated cases to the regional hospital.
- Home: recognise and report inadequately relieved pain or other physical, psychological or social distress, and improper use of morphine or other medicines; provide emotional support; educate the family on daily care (feeding, hygiene, mobility, medications).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Algorithm A: foot assessment and risk
tables.caption: Diabetic foot algorithm A: foot assessment in all patients with diabetes, active foot problems, and risk stratification (high, moderate, low) with actions
tables.content:
All patients with diabetes → foot assessment: skin; neurological; vascular; musculoskeletal.
1. Active foot problem? (any of: ulceration; spreading infection; critical limb ischaemia; gangrene; suspicion of acute Charcot neuroarthropathy or an unexplained hot, red, swollen foot with or without pain)
   - Yes → Algorithm B.
   - No → 2.
2. Previous history of ulceration, amputation, or on renal replacement therapy? Yes → HIGH RISK: early referral to podiatrist/surgical department for further care.
3. Deformity/neuropathy/non-critical limb ischaemia → MODERATE RISK: refer to NCD clinic/podiatrist/surgical department for further review.
4. Callus alone → LOW RISK: total contact insole; foot care education; yearly screening.
5. Normal findings → foot care education; yearly screening.
*Risk categories as in the diabetic foot risk stratification table.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Algorithm B: active foot problems
tables.caption: Diabetic foot algorithm B: management of active foot problems by ulcer type, infection and ischaemia (outpatient, oral antibiotics, multidisciplinary foot care team)
tables.content:
Active foot problems*:
- Without ulcer (UT grade 0): manage as outpatient by foot protection services.
- With ulcer:
  - Superficial (UT IA): manage as outpatient by foot protection services.
  - Infection:
    - Superficial ulcer not requiring surgical intervention (UT IB): oral antibiotics (outpatient, foot protection services).
    - Deep ulcer requiring surgical intervention (UT IIB/IIIB): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
  - Ischaemia (pulses not palpable) (UT IC/IIC/IIIC): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
  - Infection and ischaemia (UT ID/IID/IIID): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
*Refer urgently for admission if the patient presents with general illness (e.g. sepsis or diabetic [emergency]).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Screening > Tuning Fork Examination
tables.caption: How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy
tables.content:
1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.
2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.
3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).
4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.
5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).
6. Repeat on the other leg.
Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Key Steps in Diabetic Foot Ulcer (DFU) Management
tables.caption: Key steps in diabetic foot ulcer management: risk stratification, MDT, assessment, debridement, infection, moist healing, advanced therapies, offloading, metabolic control, monitoring, referral
tables.content:
1. Risk stratification (Wagner, UT, SINBAD).
2. Multidisciplinary team (endocrinology, podiatry, surgery, nursing, dietitian).
3. Comprehensive assessment (wound, vascular, neuropathy, labs).
4. Debridement (sharp, enzymatic, autolytic, etc.).
5. Infection management (antibiotics, osteomyelitis care).
6. Moist wound healing (appropriate dressings).
7. Advanced therapies (NPWT, skin substitutes, HBOT, PRP).
8. Offloading (total contact cast is the gold standard; walkers; footwear).
9. Glycaemic & metabolic control.
10. Monitoring & documentation (weekly to biweekly, photos).
11. Referral criteria (no healing, infection, ischaemia).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Treatment of Neuropathic Pain in Diabetic Foot
tables.caption: Treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy (flowchart): first-line anticonvulsants or antidepressants, second-line SNRIs, opioid-like drugs, topicals, third-line SSRIs and opioids
tables.content:
Patient presenting with painful neuropathy → rule out other causes of neuropathy → establish treatment goals → optimise glycaemic control.
- First-line therapy: anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin) or antidepressants (TCAs and SNRIs: amitriptyline, duloxetine).
- Second-line therapy: SNRIs (venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine); opioid-like drugs (tramadol or tapentadol ER); topical treatments (lidocaine 5% patch or capsaicin 0.075% cream).
- Third-line therapy: SSRIs (citalopram or paroxetine or escitalopram); opioids (oxycodone controlled release).
ER = extended release; SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant. Adapted from Snyder MJ, Gibbs LM, Lindsay TJ. Treating Painful Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: An Update. Am Fam Physician. 2016;94(3):227-34.
