tables.heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Screening and Diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder
tables.caption: Major depressive disorder: 8-step assessment, DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9 for 2+ weeks), severity classification and when to refer urgently
tables.content:
Assessment steps:
1. Screen: 'Have you felt sad/depressed most of the time for the past 2 weeks?' AND 'Have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?'
2. Assess core symptoms: 5 or more of 9 criteria present for 2+ weeks.
3. Assess functional impairment: work, relationships, self-care, daily activities.
4. RULE OUT: bipolar disorder (past mania?), psychosis, medical causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV, stroke, diabetes).
5. Screen for suicide/self-harm: 'Do you have thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to live?'
6. Assess alcohol and substance use (may co-occur or cause symptoms).
7. Determine severity: mild / moderate / severe (any psychotic features?).
8. DIAGNOSIS confirmed if 5+ criteria are met, at least 1 being depressed mood or anhedonia.

DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9, lasting 2+ weeks): depressed mood most of the day (or irritability in children/adolescents); markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia); significant weight loss/gain or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day; psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable by others); fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day; feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; difficulty concentrating or making decisions; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

Severity: mild – few symptoms beyond the minimum, mild functional impairment; moderate – between mild and severe, moderate impairment; severe – most symptoms, marked impairment, may have psychotic features.

When to refer urgently: active suicidal ideation with plan or intent; psychotic features (hallucinations, delusions); severe self-neglect or inability to care for self; no response after 2 adequate medication trials; suspected bipolar disorder.
tables.context_before: Screen all clients accessing services for major depressive disorder with the PHQ-9 (self-administered or by a provider).

tables.context_before: Consider antidepressants for moderate-severe depression. Discuss with the person: not addictive; takes 2-4 weeks for effect; must be taken for 9-12 months minimum after remission.
tables.table_note: Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions: depression is very common and NOT a sign of weakness or laziness; negative thoughts about self, world and future are symptoms, not reality; encourage regular activity, social engagement and pleasurable activities, regular sleep/wake times and meals; Problem Management Plus (PM+, WHO behavioural activation + problem solving); group interpersonal therapy (IPT); Thinking Healthy (CBT approach for perinatal depression); medications are NOT addictive (9-12 month course); never stop antidepressants abruptly – taper gradually. Cautions & special populations: if a manic episode occurs STOP the antidepressant immediately (may be bipolar disorder); do not combine antidepressants (serotonin syndrome); SSRIs may increase suicidal ideation in adolescents/young adults – weekly monitoring for the first 4 weeks; pregnancy: avoid if possible, if severe use the lowest effective dose with specialist input; breastfeeding: fluoxetine and sertraline generally safer; elderly: start low, go slow, monitor for falls and hyponatraemia (SSRIs); epilepsy: avoid tricyclics (lower seizure threshold).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Suicide Risk Assessment and Follow-up
tables.caption: Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening
tables.content:
SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?
- HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.
- MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.
- ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.

FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):
- Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).
- Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.
- Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).
- After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.
- 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.
- Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.

PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit.

tables.context_before: Alcohol withdrawal starts 4-12 hours after the last drink (anxiety, agitation, tremor, sympathetic activation; severe: seizures and delirium tremens, potentially fatal); symptoms may last up to 5 days. tables.table_note: Where withdrawal symptoms are present, assess severity with a validated instrument: the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, Revised (CIWA-Ar), or the self-completed 10-item Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale (SAWS).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Warning Signs of Suicidal Behaviour
tables.caption: Warning signs of suicidal behaviour
tables.content: Warning signs to look out for: feeling like a burden; being isolated; increased anxiety; talking about feeling trapped or in unbearable pain; increased substance use; looking for a way to access lethal means; increased anger or rage; extreme mood swings; expressing hopelessness and having no reason to live; sleeping too little or too much; talking or posting about wanting to die or to kill oneself; making plans for suicide; giving away prized possessions; showing rage or talking about seeking revenge; suddenly coming out of being hopeless; not wanting to complete projects one has started.
tables.context_before: Suicidal behaviour is any thought, action or behaviour indicating intent or desire to end one's life: suicidal ideation, suicide plan, suicide attempt, completed suicide. It emerges from individual, interpersonal, communal and societal factors.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Diagnostic Features of Suicidal Behaviour
tables.caption: Diagnostic features of suicidal behaviour disorder (DSM-5)
tables.content:
a. The act: 1. has been attempted within the last 24 months; 2. does not meet criteria for non-suicidal self-injury (self-injury to produce a positive mood); 3. is not applied to suicidal ideation or preparatory acts; 4. was not initiated during a state of delirium or confusion; 5. was not undertaken solely for a political or religious objective.
b. The behaviour or its consequences cause clinically significant distress or interference in interpersonal, academic, or other important areas of functioning.
c. The behaviour does not occur exclusively during psychotic episodes, delirium, substance intoxication, or substance withdrawal.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > All Age Groups – Immediate Actions and Admission Criteria
tables.caption: Acute asthma exacerbation: immediate actions for all ages (oxygen, salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids, magnesium) and admission criteria
tables.content:
All age groups – immediate actions:
- Oxygen to achieve SpO2 94–98% (adults/adolescents) or 94–98% (children).
- SABA: salbutamol 4–10 puffs via MDI + spacer every 20 min × 3 (first hour).
- Severe: nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg (children) / 5 mg (adults) every 20 min.
- Ipratropium bromide: add 0.5 mg (adults) / 0.25 mg (children) to the nebuliser for moderate–severe exacerbations.
- Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg, children) OR 40–50 mg/day (adults) × 5–7 days.
- IV magnesium sulfate: 2 g IV over 20 min (adults/adolescents) or 25–75 mg/kg (children) for severe exacerbations, SpO2 <92%.

Admission criteria – refer/admit if ANY: severe or life-threatening features; SpO2 <92% after initial treatment; no improvement after 1 hour of treatment; PEF remains <40% after initial treatment; unable to maintain oral intake (children); concern about home environment/adherence.
source_flags: The oxygen target is printed '94–98% (adults/adolescents) or 94–98% (children)' (same range twice); the primary-care flowchart on p.338 targets 93–95% in adults. Children's magnesium '25–75 mg/kg' is printed (usually 25–50 mg/kg, max 2 g).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > Management of acute asthma in primary care
tables.caption: Acute or sub-acute asthma exacerbation in primary care (flowchart): assessment, severity (mild/moderate, severe, life-threatening), treatment, transfer, discharge and follow-up
tables.content:
1. Patient presents with an acute or sub-acute asthma exacerbation. Assess: is it asthma? Risk factors for asthma-related death? Severity of the exacerbation?
2. Severity:
   - Mild or moderate: talks in phrases; prefers sitting to lying; not agitated; respiratory rate increased; accessory muscles used; pulse 100-120 bpm; O2 saturation (on air) 90-95%; PEF >50% predicted or best (printed '50%').
   - Severe: talks in words; sits hunched; agitated; respiratory rate >30/min; accessory muscles used; pulse >120/min; O2 saturation (on air) <90%; PEF <50% predicted or best.
   - Life-threatening: drowsy; confused; silent chest.
3. Mild/moderate: start treatment: SABA 4-10 puffs by pMDI + spacer, repeat every 20 min for 1 hour; prednisolone adults 40-50 mg, children 1-2 mg/kg (max 40 mg); controlled oxygen (if available), target saturation 93-95% (children 94-98%).
   - Worsening → transfer to an acute care facility.
   - Improving → continue SABA as needed; assess response at 1 hour (or earlier).
4. Severe or life-threatening → transfer to an acute care facility; while waiting give SABA, ipratropium bromide, oxygen, systemic corticosteroids.
5. Assess for discharge: symptoms improved, SABA not needed; PEF improving and >60-80% of personal best or predicted; oxygen saturation >94% on room air; adequate resources at home.
6. Follow-up: review symptoms and signs (is the exacerbation resolving? should prednisolone be continued?). Reliever: reduce to as needed. Controller: continue a higher dose short term (1-2 weeks) or long term (3 months) depending on the background to the exacerbation. Risk factors: check and correct modifiable risk factors, including inhaler technique and adherence; refer if >1-2 exacerbations.
source_flags: Severity thresholds here (SpO2 90-95% mild/moderate, <90% severe; PEF 50%) differ from the severity table on p.334 (SpO2 92-94% moderate, <92% severe; PEF 40-69% moderate, <40% severe). 'Life threating', 'Ipratroplum', 'on aur' printed.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations (adults, adolescents, children 6-11)
tables.caption: Management of acute asthma exacerbations in adults, adolescents and children 6-11 (flowchart): triage by worst feature, treatment, reassessment at 1 hour; IV salbutamol and aminophylline
tables.content:
1. Initial assessment: A airway, B breathing, C circulation. Any of drowsiness, confusion, silent chest? → consult ICU, start SABA and O2, and prepare the patient for intubation.
2. Further triage by clinical status, according to the worst feature:
   - Mild or moderate: talks in phrases; prefers sitting to lying down; not agitated; respiratory rate increased; accessory muscles not used; pulse rate 100-120 bpm (printed '100-200'); O2 saturation (on air) 90-95%; PEF >50% predicted or best. Treat: short-acting beta agonists; O2 to maintain saturation 94-98%; oral corticosteroids.
   - Severe: talks in words; sits hunched forwards; agitated; respiratory rate >30/min; accessory muscles being used; pulse rate >120 bpm; O2 saturation (on air) <90%; PEF <50% predicted or best. Treat: short-acting beta2 agonists; ipratropium bromide; O2 to maintain saturation 94-98%; oral or IV corticosteroids; consider IV magnesium sulfate; IV terbutaline/IV aminophylline.
   - If continuing deterioration, treat as severe and reassess for ICU; transfer if necessary.
3. Assess clinical progress frequently; measure lung function in all patients one hour after initial treatment:
   - FEV1 or PEF 60-80% of predicted or personal best and symptoms improved (moderate): consider discharge.
   - FEV1 or PEF <60% of predicted or personal best, or lack of clinical response (severe): continue treatment as above and reassess frequently.

IV salbutamol can be used in severe asthma failing other treatments, mainly to prevent intubation; evidence that IV beta2-agonists shorten recovery or improve lung function is very limited. Inhaled drugs may have limited effect with near-complete obstruction and in ventilated patients. Side effects: arrhythmia, tachycardia, raised lactate and anxiety (may increase respiratory workload). Patients on IV salbutamol should be in an ICU setting.
Most guidelines do not recommend IV aminophylline (low efficacy and safety). If used, reserve it for severe exacerbations failing maximal therapy (continuous inhaled beta2-agonists, IV corticosteroids, IV magnesium sulfate), generally in high care/ICU. Its risk-benefit balance is unfavourable.
source_flags: Mild/moderate pulse rate is printed '100-200 bpm' (100-120 on p.338). IV terbutaline/aminophylline are listed in the severe treatment box although the text below says aminophylline is generally not recommended.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease > Symptoms and Signs
tables.caption: COPD clinical features: chronic cough, sputum, acute bronchitis, dyspnoea, exposure history, advanced disease features, physical signs

body.t: Persistent, intermittently or every day; often present throughout the day, seldom only nocturnal
Any pattern of chronic sputum production may indicate COPD
Progressive; persistent; worse with exercise; worse during respiratory infections
History of exposure to risk factors
Tobacco smoke; occupational dusts and chemicals; indoor and outdoor pollution

Tachypnoea; reduced chest expansion; hyperinflated lungs; hyper-resonant percussion; use of accessory respiratory muscles and paradoxical indrawing of lower intercostal spaces (Hoover sign); cyanosis (blue bloater) – oedematous and central cyanosis; pink puffer – always breathless; elevated JVP; peripheral oedema; wheezing on forced and unforced expiration; diffusely decreased breath sounds; signs of respiratory failure; signs of cor pulmonale

footnotes: Signs may be completely absent in early stages of COPD.
tables.context_before: COPD: a slowly progressive group of disorders with airway inflammation and airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. Two types: chronic bronchitis (productive cough for at least 3 months a year for more than 2 consecutive years) and emphysema (pathological diagnosis: abnormal dilation of terminal air spaces with destruction of alveolar septa). Risk factors: smoking; indoor and outdoor air pollution; recurrent childhood respiratory infection; occupational; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; genetic predisposition.

body.t: Not troubled by breathlessness except on strenuous exercise
Short of breath when hurrying or walking up a slight hill

source_flags: FEV1 ≥80% is not covered (GOLD grades: mild ≥80%, moderate 50-79%, severe 30-49%, very severe <30%); the bands here differ from GOLD.
tables.context_before: Spirometry is the gold standard for diagnosis, assessment and management of COPD. A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 confirms persistent airflow limitation, suggesting COPD with relevant symptoms; FEV1 <80% predicted indicates the severity of obstruction. Measure after a bronchodilator to help distinguish from asthma. Other tests: CXR, high-resolution CT.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease > Step-Wise Management for COPD: Pharmacological Interventions
tables.caption: Stepwise pharmacological management of COPD: short-acting bronchodilators, combinations, long-acting bronchodilator, ICS, theophylline; asthma-COPD overlap
tables.content:
Non-pharmacological: smoking cessation and/or nicotine replacement therapy.
1. Start a short-acting bronchodilator for relief of breathlessness: beta2 agonist, e.g. salbutamol 100-200 mcg (1-2 puffs) as needed, OR anticholinergic, e.g. ipratropium 20-40 mcg 3-4 times a day.
2. Poor symptom control → combine short-acting bronchodilators from different groups, e.g. salbutamol and ipratropium (as above).
3. Poor symptom control → consider adding a long-acting bronchodilator (beta2 agonist or anticholinergic), e.g. salmeterol 50 mcg BD, with short-acting bronchodilator(s) as above.
4. Poor symptom control → consider combining a long-acting bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid, e.g. beclomethasone 200 mcg, with a short-acting bronchodilator. Discontinue corticosteroids after 4 weeks if no benefit.
5. Poor symptom control → consider adding SR theophylline 250-500 mg BD; monitor plasma levels and interactions.

Asthma-COPD overlap, initial treatment: predominant asthma features → inhaled corticosteroids (long-acting bronchodilators should not be used as monotherapy). Predominant COPD features → appropriate long-acting bronchodilators; consider ICS + long-acting bronchodilator combination; ICS should not be used as monotherapy for COPD.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Bronchiectasis > Bronchiectasis: features and management
tables.caption: Bronchiectasis: predisposing factors, symptoms, imaging findings, complications, differential diagnosis, and management (non-pharmacological, acute, chronic, referral)

body.t: Infectious: whooping cough, measles, tuberculosis. Obstructive: inhaled foreign body, bronchial carcinoma. Genetic/congenital: cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome

Daily cough, worse on walking. Mild cases: yellow or green sputum only after infection. Advanced: daily profuse sputum; persistent halitosis; haemoptysis (occasional and recurrent); shortness of breath and wheezing; recurrent chest infections; fevers and/or chills

Tram tracks (dilated airways), signet-ring sign, lack of bronchial tapering, cystic lesions at the lung bases in some patients. The gold standard for diagnosis is high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT)
Pneumonia, pleurisy, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, sinusitis, haemoptysis (>600 mL/day = life-threatening), brain abscess
Tuberculosis, asthma, COPD, interstitial fibrosis, chronic lung abscess, foreign body aspiration, cystic fibrosis, lung carcinoma
Postural drainage (e.g. lie head down 10–20 min ×3/day), adequate hydration, supplemental oxygen, patient education & preventive care
Antibiotics guided by Gram stain; target common pathogens (H. influenzae, P. aeruginosa if unknown); bronchodilators if bronchospasm present
Avoid tobacco; maintain nutrition & hydration; prompt treatment of infections; vaccination (pneumococcal, influenza)
Consider partial lung resection for severe cases unresponsive to medical therapy

tables.context_before: Bronchiectasis: dilation of the bronchi when their walls become inflamed, thickened and irreversibly damaged, usually after obstruction followed by infection. The left lower lobe and lingula are the commonest sites of localized disease.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Bronchiectasis > Diagnosis and management algorithm
tables.caption: Bronchiectasis diagnosis and management (flowchart): chest X-ray, CT, routine and further tests, cause-specific and general management
tables.content:
Risk factors, symptoms and/or signs suggestive of bronchiectasis? → request a chest X-ray.
- Chest X-ray in keeping with bronchiectasis? Yes → bronchiectasis confirmed. No → request thin-slice CT chest or high-resolution CT.
- CT chest in keeping with bronchiectasis? Yes → bronchiectasis confirmed. No → consider an alternative diagnosis.
Once confirmed:
- Routine tests: FBC, U&E and creatinine, LFTs, glucose, HIV, sputum MCS and TB culture, Aspergillus IgE, sweat chloride.
- Further tests guided by history and examination: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgG subclasses, total IgE, sweat conductivity, nasal or bronchial mucosa biopsy.
- If an underlying cause is identified, treat it specifically.
- General management: airway clearance techniques; vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, SARS-CoV-2); antibiotics; other: nutrition, diuretics, lung transplant.
source_flags: 'Asperillus', 'or conductivity' printed.

tables.context_before: Haematuria is the presence of blood in urine, grossly or microscopically. It is a sign rather than a condition, usually suggesting a condition of the genito-urinary tract that needs urgent attention.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Hematuria > Management of Gross Hematuria
tables.caption: Management of gross haematuria by pathway: haemodynamically unstable, stable with clot retention, stable without clot retention

body.t: Suprapubic pain, bladder distension, inability to void
Investigate cause. Send urine for M/C/S. If terminal hematuria, send a specimen between 10am and 2pm to look for schistosomiasis and treat accordingly

tables.context_before: Initial management (clinic, health centre or hospital): ATLS approach; fluid therapy, blood transfusions; correct reversible derangements (infections, coagulopathies); indwelling 3-way catheter (22/24 Fr); clot evacuation and bladder irrigation with isotonic saline (60 cc catheter-tip syringes, 3 L saline bags/water for irrigation); once stabilised, refer to a urologist.
tables.table_note: ALL CLIENTS PRESENTING WITH GROSS HEMATURIA SHOULD BE REFERRED TO THE UROLOGIST.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Hematuria > Management of Microhematuria
tables.caption: Management of microscopic haematuria (flowchart): confirm, infection, glomerular cause, other causes, imaging, cytology, cystoscopy, follow-up
tables.content:
1. Microscopic evaluation to confirm RBCs (>3 RBC/HPF) in 2 of 3 samples.
2. Signs or symptoms of infection (dysuria, frequency, flank pain, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, white cells, bacteria)?
   - Yes: treat the infection; confirm resolution of microscopic haematuria with a follow-up urinalysis 6 weeks after completing therapy.
   - No: 3.
3. Findings supporting a glomerular cause (proteinuria, elevated creatinine, red cell casts, dysmorphic RBCs, abnormal sediment, ≥5-10 WBC/HPF, or reduced renal function)? Yes: refer to a nephrologist. (Cytology is a poor screening test and is not recommended in the initial workup.)
4. No: other aetiology probable (vigorous exercise, urethral trauma, menstruation, offending medication)? Yes: retest urine after the possible contributing factor is stopped.
5. No: radiographic evaluation of the urinary tract (renal ultrasonography, CT, or IVP, considering availability and costs). If imaging is not available, refer to a urologist.
   - If imaging is positive: refer to a urology subspecialist. If negative: urine cytology.
   - Negative findings and low risk (age <40 and no risk factors): follow-up with urinalysis and blood pressure; if haematuria persists >3 months, consider specialist referral.
   - Positive findings, or all patients >40, or younger patients with risk factors for urothelial tumours: refer to a urology subspecialist for cystoscopy.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Adult Male LUTS / Haematuria / Retention - Clinical Algorithm
tables.caption: Adult male with LUTS, haematuria or urinary retention: assessment pathway, red flags, medical treatment vs emergency care, refer to urologist
tables.content:
Step 1–5: assessment pathway
1. Adult male with LUTS ± haematuria / retention.
2. History: LUTS, haematuria, retention; comorbidities, medications.
3. IPSS ± IIEF.
4. Examination: abdominal, neurological, DRE.
5. Investigations: urine dipstick ± MCS; FBC, UECs, PSA; KUB ± prostate ultrasound.
Decision: red flags present?
- No red flags: medical treatment – alpha-blocker ± 5-ARI, monitor IPSS → refer if poor response.
- Red flags present: emergency care – 3-way catheter 22–24 Fr, irrigation ± clot evacuation → stabilise.
Both pathways: refer to urologist.
Key: IPSS = International Prostate Symptom Score; IIEF = International Index of Erectile Function; DRE = digital rectal examination; FBC = full blood count; UECs = urea, electrolytes & creatinine; PSA = prostate-specific antigen; MCS = microscopy, culture & sensitivity; KUB = kidneys, ureters & bladder X-ray; 5-ARI = 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; USS = ultrasound scan; LUTS = lower urinary tract symptoms.
source_flags: The red-flag criteria themselves are not listed on the algorithm.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Benign Prostatic Uropathy > Standard Classification of Benign Prostatic Uropathy
tables.caption: Standard classification and terminology of benign prostatic uropathy: BOO, BPH, BPE, BPO definitions

body.t: A generic clinical term for a blockage that slows or stops urine flow during voiding.
Diagnosed via urodynamics (shows high bladder pressure but low flow).
A histological (microscopic) diagnosis referring to the overgrowth of prostate cells.
It is a cellular diagnosis, typically confirmed through biopsy or pathology after surgery.
A clinical observation of an increased prostate volume (size), regardless of symptoms.
Can be detected via physical exam (digital rectal exam) or imaging (ultrasound).
A specific form of BOO where the blockage is proven to be caused by BPE.
This links the physical size of the prostate to the actual obstruction of urine.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Benign Prostatic Uropathy > Benign Prostatic Obstructive Uropathy > Treatment
tables.caption: Treatment of benign prostatic obstruction / BPH by line of therapy: watchful waiting, urotherapy and lifestyle, alpha-1 blockers tamsulosin and doxazosin, side effects, referral and follow-up

body.t: BPE without bothersome symptoms – mild IPSS score
Watchful waiting (mild IPSS): reassure, reinforce healthy lifestyle
Education and lifestyle modification are central

- Urotherapy: double voiding
- Treat constipation
- Bladder training
- Urethral milking post-void
- Control fluid intake (storage LUTS)

- Avoid bladder irritants (coffee, alcohol, cola, spicy foods)
- Optimise DM/HTN control if concomitant
- Substitute LUTS-exacerbating drugs (diuretics, TCAs, antihistamines, flu medications)
Alpha-1 blockers – relax internal sphincter & prostate smooth muscles
Tamsulosin (Uromax) 0.4 mg OD (may double in selected cases) – uroselective

- Retrograde ejaculation → ↓ ejaculate volume
- Orthostatic hypotension (first few weeks) → ↑ fall risk
- Floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery → avoid in cataract patients
Particularly useful in patients with hypertension

- Dizziness
- Asthenia
- Orthostatic hypotension
- Strong vasodilatory effect → avoid with nitrates or CCF

tables.table_note: Patients whose IPSS fails to improve despite the interventions above are candidates for referral to a urologist for further evaluation, with the possibility of combination therapy or surgical treatment. Patients doing well on therapy can be seen at 3–6-month intervals.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Erectile Function Disorders > Guidelines for Primary Care Management of Erectile Dysfunction
tables.caption: Primary care management of erectile dysfunction (flowchart): initial assessment, psychogenic vs organic features, investigations, hypogonadism, PDE5 inhibitors, CHD, referral
tables.content:
1. GP initial assessment: sexual history, relevant blood tests, blood pressure, genital examination. ALL young patients with a history of trauma and/or penile/testicular abnormalities on clinical examination SHOULD BE REFERRED TO UROLOGY IMMEDIATELY.
2a. Suggests psychogenic: sudden onset; good or better early-morning / self-stimulated erections; relationship problems; variable depending on circumstances → first-line treatment with PDE5 inhibitors and monitor response; consider counselling.
2b. Suggests organic: gradual onset; lack of tumescence; normal libido; relevant medical history; smoker; difficulty with penetration → further investigations: BMI, BP, abdominal circumference, HbA1c, lipogram; encourage weight loss.
3. Clinical features suggestive of hypogonadism: testosterone (before 10 am) and thyroid function; if testosterone low, do FSH, LH, prolactin, SHBG.
   - If abnormal: refer to urology / endocrinology as appropriate.
   - If normal with no evidence of CHD: first-line treatment with PDE5 inhibitors.
   - Normal but with CHD: guidance from cardiology/medicine; once the patient is low risk according to Princeton criteria, consider PDE5 inhibitors.
PDE5 inhibitors: sildenafil (Viagra); tadalafil (Cialis) – consider daily dose if possible; vardenafil (Levitra).
source_flags: Printed 'IF NORMAL WITH N EVIDENCE OF CHD' (read as 'no evidence'), 'Tadalifil', 'In hibitors', 'Princetown' (Princeton), 'SHOULD REFERRED'.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Erectile Function Disorders > PDE5 Inhibitors
tables.caption: PDE5 inhibitors for erectile dysfunction: sildenafil (Viagra) vs tadalafil (Cialis) onset, half-life, food effect, doses, side effects, contraindications, pharmacological failure

body.t: Headache, dyspepsia, facial flushing, blurred/blue vision (rare), myalgia, backache

Counsel the patient to take the medication at least 8 times at the maximum dose, 1 hour before sex, on an empty stomach, together with sexual stimulation, before it is deemed medication failure. Then refer to urology.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Erectile Function Disorders > PDE5 Inhibitor Eligibility (Princeton III)
tables.caption: PDE5 inhibitor fitness/eligibility by cardiovascular risk (Princeton III Consensus 2010): low, intermediate, high risk and management

body.t:
- Controlled hypertension
- Successfully revascularised (e.g. bypass surgery)

- Mild or moderate stable angina
- Past myocardial infarction (2–8 weeks)
Cardiovascular evaluation & management → if improves: low-risk management; if fails: high-risk management (refer to cardiologist / internal medicine)

- Unstable angina
- CCF NYHA IV
- Recent MI (<2 weeks)

tables.context_before: PDE5 inhibitors' fitness/eligibility criteria – based on the Princeton III Consensus Conference 2010.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 15: Urology > Erectile Function Disorders > Premature Ejaculation
tables.caption: Premature ejaculation: types (lifelong/primary vs acquired/secondary), description and aetiology

body.t: Cluster of core symptoms including early ejaculation at nearly every intercourse: within 30–60 seconds in ~80% of cases; between 1–2 minutes in ~20% of cases
Early ejaculation at some point in life in men who previously had normal ejaculatory experiences
